title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 52
paragraphs: As to this road, the truth is as follows. Everywhere there are royal stages and excellent rest-houses, and the whole road runs through inhabited and safe country. Through Lydia and Phrygia there extend twenty stages, amounting to ninety-four and a half leagues; and after Phrygia comes the river Halys, at which there is a gate that one must pass through in order to cross the river, and a strong guard-post is established there. Then, after crossing into Cappadocia, it is twenty-eight stages, being one hundred and four leagues, by this road to the borders of Cilicia; and on the Cilician frontier you pass through two separate gates and go by two separate guard-posts. After passing these, it is three stages, amounting to fifteen and a half leagues, to journey through Cilicia; and the boundary of Cilicia and Armenia is a navigable river called the Euphrates. In Armenia the number of stages with rest-houses is fifteen, and the number of leagues fifty-six and a half, and there is a guard-post on the way. From Armenia, when one enters the land of Matiene, there are thirty-four stages, amounting to one hundred and thirty-seven leagues; and through this land flow four navigable rivers, which cannot be crossed except by ferries—first the Tigris, then a second and a third, both called by the same name, though they are not the same river nor do they flow from the same region (the first of them flows from the Armenian land and the other from that of the Matieni), and the fourth of these rivers is called the Gyndes, the same river that Cyrus once divided into three hundred and sixty channels. Passing thence into the Cissian land, there are eleven stages, forty-two and a half leagues, to the river Choaspes, which is also navigable; and on this is built the city of Susa. The total number of stages comes to one hundred and eleven.
